newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to talk with Iraq on gas purchases.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to talk with Iraq on gas purchases.

text.p: Turkish Energy Minister Recai Kutan will visit Iraq on May 7-11 for talks on a proposed deal for Turkey to develop Iraqi gas fields and buy gas through a pipeline, the energy ministry said on Tuesday.
"The minister is going to Baghdad to have talks on natural gas and oil," said the statement, which gave no other details.
Turkey and Iraq have already discussed details of the project during talks in December and April, despite U.N. trade sanctions on Baghdad imposed because of its invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
An aide to Kutan said the deal would entail building a pipeline of 1,300 km to 1,800 km from Iraq to Turkey with an annual capacity of 10 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas.
"The cost of the pipeline will be around $2.5 billion," he told Reuters. He said the route would be determined during the talks in Baghdad.

According to the deal, Turkey's state oil and natural gas explorer and producer TPAO, pipeline company Botas and Iraq would jointly carry out exploration, possibly near Al-Anfal gas fields, which produce 5.6 million cubic metres a day, he said.
Iraqi officials said last month the two countries would sign an agreement in June or July to seal the deal, which Turkey has said would not breach the U.N. embargo.

Turkish officials did not say when the deal would go into effect. But analysts say Turkey cannot get Iraqi gas before the U.N. lifts sanctions, which is not expected to happen soon despite periodic U.N. reviews.
The world body has said the sanctions will remain in place until it is fully satisfied that Iraq does not hide any weapons of mass destruction.
The United Nations last year allowed Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine. The deal ends in June but may be extended for a further six months.

In a bid to lessen its dependence on coal and oil, and to diversify gas resources, Turkey has signed several gas deals with nearby suppliers as well as buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from countries as far away as Nigeria and Algeria.
It currently buys gas from Russia and Algeria. Its recent deals include agreements for further gas from Russia and purchases from Turkmenistan, Iran, Nigeria, Yemen and Qatar.
Turkey uses about nine bcm of natural gas a year, of which six bcm come from Russia. Its needs will reach 27 bmc in 2000 and 60 bmc by 2010, according to official projections.
